title: Zero-Inflated / Hurdle Count Regression
countformula: Count model formula (predicts the count, including zeros)
inflationformula: Zero-inflation / hurdle formula (predicts always-zero vs. not, or zero vs. positive)
hurdle: Hurdle (two-part: zero vs. positive, then truncated count)
zeroLinkLabel: Link function for the zero/hurdle part
expCoefficients: Exponentiate coefficients (IRR for count part, OR for zero/hurdle part)

help.title: Zero-Inflated / Hurdle Count Regression
help.body:
Description
Fits count regression models for outcomes with more zeros than a standard Poisson or Negative Binomial model would predict.

Zero-inflated models (pscl::zeroinfl) assume the zeros come from a mixture of two sources: "structural" zeros from observations that can never generate a positive count, and "sampling" zeros from the ordinary count process. A binary model (logit/probit/cloglog) predicts which observations are structural zeros; a Poisson or Negative Binomial model predicts the count (including possible zeros) for everyone else.

Hurdle models (pscl::hurdle) instead assume a single binary process governs whether the count is zero or positive (the "hurdle"). Conditional on crossing the hurdle, a zero-truncated Poisson or Negative Binomial model governs the positive counts.

Specify two formulas: the count model formula (right-hand side predictors for the count process) and the zero-inflation/hurdle formula (right-hand side predictors for the binary process). Internally this builds y ~ countformula | inflationformula.

NOTE 1: Unlike the standard GLM dialog, the theoretical model equation is not displayed because the equatiomatic package does not support zeroinfl/hurdle objects. The fitted formula is printed instead.
NOTE 2: An "Observed vs Expected Zero Counts" table is displayed after fitting. If your data has many more zeros than a plain Poisson/Negative Binomial GLM would predict, that is the signal to use this dialog instead of the standard GLM dialog.
NOTE 3: When specifying a variable containing weights, be aware that since we use the option na.exclude to build the model, all NA values are automatically removed from the dependent and independent variables. NA values are NOT automatically removed from the weighting variable, which can cause a "variable lengths differ (found for (weights))" error. To fix, go to Variables>Missing Values>Remove NAs and select the dependent, independent, and weighting variables first.
Usage
zeroinfl(formula, data, weights, offset, dist = "poisson", link = "logit", na.action = na.exclude, ...)
hurdle(formula, data, weights, offset, dist = "poisson", zero.dist = "binomial", link = "logit", na.action = na.exclude, ...)
Arguments
  • formula: a formula of the form y ~ x1 + x2 | z1 + z2. The part before | specifies the count model; the part after | specifies the zero-inflation (or hurdle) model. If no | is used, the same predictors are used for both parts.
  • dist: distribution for the count component: "poisson", "negbin", or "geometric".
  • link (zeroinfl): link function for the zero-inflation binary model: "logit", "probit", "cloglog", "cauchit", "log".
  • zero.dist / link (hurdle): distribution and link for the hurdle component. This dialog uses the common "binomial" hurdle with a selectable link.
  • data: an optional data frame containing the variables in the model.
  • weights: an optional vector of prior weights.
  • offset: an optional numeric vector added to the linear predictor of the count model.
  • na.action: a function indicating what should happen when data contain NAs. na.exclude is used here.
Value
An object of class "zeroinfl" or "hurdle", a list containing (among others):
  • coefficients: a list with count and zero model coefficient vectors.
  • residuals: raw residuals on the response scale.
  • fitted.values: fitted mean values, obtained by taking the expectation of the fitted mixture/hurdle distribution.
  • loglik: the log-likelihood of the fitted model.
  • vcov: the estimated covariance matrix.
Package
pscl
Help
help(zeroinfl, package ='pscl') and help(hurdle, package ='pscl')

Worked examples using the test dataset (manufacturing_count_data_with_answers.xlsx)
This workbook has two data sheets, each built to demonstrate one of the two model types. Open the sheet as the active dataset before opening this dialog.

Example 1 — Sheet "MachineBreakdowns" (Zero-Inflated)
Many weeks are structural zeros (the line simply wasn't running, or the machine was effectively not at risk that week); other zeros are genuine low-risk weeks. This is a Zero-Inflated scenario.
  • Model name: ZeroInflModel1 (or any name you like)
  • Dependent variable: Breakdowns
  • Count model formula: MachineAgeYears + DaysSincePM + OperatorExperienceYears + MachineType
  • Zero-inflation / hurdle formula: MachineAgeYears + DaysSincePM + OperatorExperienceYears
  • Offset: leave blank
  • Weights: leave blank
  • Model type: check Zero-inflated
  • Count model distribution: check Negative Binomial (this data is overdispersed)
  • Link function for the zero/hurdle part: check Logit
  • Exponentiate coefficients: optional — check it only if you want IRR/OR tables in addition to the raw coefficient tables
Example 2 — Sheet "BatchScrap" (Hurdle)
No batch is "immune" to scrap; whether any scrap occurs at all is governed by incoming material lot grade and shift, while the amount of scrap, given it occurs, is governed by machine setting drift and batch size. This is a Hurdle scenario.
  • Model name: HurdleModel1 (or any name you like)
  • Dependent variable: ScrapUnits
  • Count model formula: MachineSettingDeviation + BatchSizeUnits
  • Zero-inflation / hurdle formula: MaterialLotGrade + OperatorShift
  • Offset: leave blank
  • Weights: leave blank
  • Model type: check Hurdle
  • Count model distribution: check Poisson
  • Link function for the zero/hurdle part: check Logit
  • Exponentiate coefficients: optional, same as above
NOTE: never combine models built on these two sheets in the same later model-comparison step — they have different sample sizes (520 vs. 480 rows), so tools such as the Vuong test will correctly refuse to compare them.
